Level
Tags: programs,specializations
Short Description: The academic level of a curricular offering (undergraduate / graduate / dual)
Level
Level identifies the academic level of a curricular offering.

Undergraduate: Courses numbered 499 and below.
Graduate — Courses numbered 500 and above.

Undergraduate: A program leading to an undergraduate degree or credential, such as a bachelor’s degree, undergraduate certificate, or minor.
Graduate: A program designed for students who have completed a bachelor’s degree and are pursuing graduate or post-baccalaureate study, including master’s degrees, doctoral degrees, graduate certificates, and other post-baccalaureate credentials.

In addition to undergraduate and graduate, proposers may select Dual for programs that provide an accelerated pathway connecting a bachelor's and master's degree, including ABM and 4+1 specializations.
Related toolkit entry: ABM
Related toolkit entry: 4+1
ABM (Accelerated Bachelor to Master's): A pathway that allows students to double-count eligible courses toward both the bachelor's and master's degrees, reducing the time required to complete the master's degree
Kuali: ABM programs are inherited from the master's degree.
4+1: A pathway that allows students to complete both a bachelor's and master's degree in five years. Unlike an ABM, a 4+1 does not include double-counted courses.
Kuali: 4+1s are inherited from the bachelors degree.

Syllabus
Tags: courses
Short Description: A roadmap for a course that communicates its scope, learning outcomes, expectations, policies, assessments, and other essential information students need to successfully complete the course.
Syllabus
University Manual 8.50.30 Course Syllabi. All instructors shall make available a syllabus in the first week of class, or first day of class for fully-online accelerated programs (8.51.24), to students enrolled in each of their courses. Syllabi components should clearly communicate classroom policies, essential aspects of the course, and expectations of student participation.
University Manual 8.51.24 For online courses taught in the fully-online accelerated calendar, final projects and/or final exams shall be scheduled by faculty according to the learning outcomes of the class and best pedagogical practices for online learning. The calendar of due dates for assignments and assessments shall be in the syllabus and available to students on the first day of class. No final exam or final project shall be due after the last day of the session.
From the Provost:

In addition to satisfying Faculty Senate approved policies, your syllabus communicates mutual expectations between you and your students and serves as a roadmap to successful course completion, including your course scope, expectations, learning outcomes, deadlines, attendance policies, grading criteria, and other important information. Please provide students with information about assessment/major paper/project due dates, office hours, availability of special tutorial sessions, and expectations on individual vs group work. This clear outlining of expectations helps to ensure that students in your classes understand what they are expected to learn, how they will be assessed, and are fully aware of your academic standards. Providing such information can help avoid misunderstanding, frustration—on both sides—and foster acceptance of responsibility by our students

The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program.
Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.

Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the program to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.

Important Information about Changing a Program’s Academic Calendar
If a program is currently offered on the Traditional Academic Calendar and you would like to move it to the Accelerated Academic Calendar, you cannot simply change the calendar while students are still enrolled in the program. The existing program must first be fully taught out. This requires a proposal to suspend admission to the program. Once there are no students remaining in the program, the program can be moved from one academic calendar to the other.

Alternatively, you may propose a new program by cloning the existing program. This approach does not require Board of Trustees approval and is treated as a program modification. Creating a separate program allows students to be appropriately coded according to the academic calendar in which their program is offered (Traditional or Accelerated).

Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
How to input Courses Approved for Double Counting in your ABM Specialization form.
Whether you are creating a new ABM, or modifying an existing, you will be asked to input all courses approved for double counting in a “Rules” gadget.

Click Use Rule Categories checkbox
Click + Add Rules
In the blank box next to A, click the drop-down carrot, and select Double-Count.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select minimum number of credits from.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select selected courses.
Enter the total number of double-counted course credits in the Credits box. In the Courses box, list all courses that may be used toward these credits.
If the ABM allows only a certain number of credits from the courses specified, you can end here and move on to the next section of your form.

If you would like to add a statement indicating that other courses may be considered for double-counting with input from an advisor, program director, or other appropriate individual, follow these steps:
Click the plus (+) sign underneath the blue Update Logic button.
You will now see a blank box labeled with the letter B. In this box, click the drop-down carrot, and select Free form text.
Enter the text to accompany the courses selected.
Text Examples:
“Other 400-level ENG courses approved for graduate credit may be chosen in consultation with the program director.”
“Any 500-level CSF course approved by the advisor.”
“Nine credits may be double counted for the ABM Degree. Only 500­-level courses and 400­-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.”

Temporary Course
Tags: courses
Short Description: A course approved for limited offerings, typically to test an experimental course or address a temporary need. Also known as an “X-Course.”
Temporary Course
UM 8.80.12 A temporary course may be offered no more than twice and only during a two-year period following its approval. A temporary course must meet one or more of the following criteria: a) it is experimental in nature. It is innovative, using unconventional devices or pedagogical methods, course materials, approach to course content or student-teacher relationships; b) it is being tried out on a temporary basis so that its value and effectiveness can be tested before it is added to a department’s permanent curriculum; c) it is intended for a limited duration, such as in the case of employing a visiting specialist temporarily available or to satisfy temporary needs and interests of students or to deal with timely issues.

UM 8.81.30 A Temporary Course shall have approval of the department(s) or committee proposing it, the dean(s) of the college(s) involved, and the Curriculum and Standards Committee and/or the Graduate Council, except that a temporary University College mini-course (a one-credit lower-level undergraduate course taught during the fall or spring semester) does not require the approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee. The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall, however, receive information about any temporary University College mini-course after it has been approved by the college dean. The Graduate Council may refuse to grant or may attach conditions to the granting of graduate program credit for a temporary course. Each college may require internal channels of approval in addition to those specified here.

UM 8.81.31 The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the Graduate Council shall give priority at their meetings to the consideration of proposed temporary courses. Prior to approving temporary courses, these committees shall distribute to all faculty a description of these courses and shall provide faculty members with a seven-day period in which to register comments with the Chairperson of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and/or with the Dean of the Graduate School.
UM 8.81.60 It is the responsibility of the Office of Enrollment Services to limit the offering of a temporary course to only twice during a two-year period and to limit to three times the offering of a specific topic within an open-ended course.
